<context>
You are an expert at solving ARC-AGI (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus) puzzles using Answer Set Programming (ASP).

ARC-AGI puzzles show input-output grid transformations. Each cell contains a color value (integer 0–9). The goal is to discover the hidden transformation rule from training examples and encode it as an ASP program.
</context>

<rules>
- `input(row, col, color)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- `color(0..9)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- the output predicate is always `output(row, col, color)` — do not redefine it.
- the final program must produce exactly one answer set, in which `output(row, col, color)` match the expected output exactly.
- end your program with `#show output/3.`
</rules>

<example_1>
This puzzle copies the input to the output unchanged.

<grid_1>
Input:
<diagram>
0 1 0
2 0 3
0 4 0
</diagram>

Output:
<diagram>
0 1 0
2 0 3
0 4 0
</diagram>
</grid_1>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Each output cell gets exactly one color
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Copy each input cell to the output unchanged
output(R, C, Color) :- input(R, C, Color).

#show output/3.
</asp>
</example_1>

<example_2>
This puzzle replaces every non-zero cell with color 5; zero cells stay 0.

<grid_1>
Input:
<diagram>
0 1 0
2 0 3
0 4 0
</diagram>

Output:
<diagram>
0 5 0
5 0 5
0 5 0
</diagram>
</grid_1>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Each output cell gets exactly one color
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Recolor every non-zero cell to 5; zeros stay 0.
output(R, C, 5) :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.
output(R, C, 0) :- input(R, C, 0).

#show output/3.
</asp>
</example_2>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Each output cell gets exactly one color
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Mirror: column C of the output is column (M-1-C) of the input.
output(R, C, Color) :- input(R, Cin, Color), n_cols(M), C = M - 1 - Cin.

#show output/3.
</asp>
</example_3>

n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, 0, 0) }.
n_cols(M) :- M = #count{ C : input(0, C, 0) }.

maxC(Cmax) :- Cmax = #max{ C : input(R, C, X), X != 0 }.

core_col(C) :- col(C), C > minC, C < maxC.

% Determine rows and columns that contain a non‑zero cell
row_nonzero(R) :- input(R, _, X), X != 0.
col_nonzero(C) :- input(_, C, X), X != 0.

% Bounding rectangle of all non‑zero cells
Rmin := #min{R : row_nonzero(R)}.
Rmax := #max{R : row_nonzero(R)}.
Cmin := #min{C : col_nonzero(C)}.
Cmax := #max{C : col_nonzero(C)}.

% Maximal colour in the whole grid
maxc(M) :- color(M), M != 0, M = #max{X : color(X), X != 0, input(_, _, X)}.

% Second maximal colour (0 if none)
secondc(S) :- color(S), color(M), S != M, S != 0,
               S = #max{X : color(X), X != 0, X != M, input(_, _, X)}.

% The maximal colour occupies all four corners of the bounding rectangle?
corner_maxc :-
    input(Rmin, Cmin, maxc),
    input(Rmin, Cmax, maxc),
    input(Rmax, Cmin, maxc),
    input(Rmax, Cmax, maxc).

% Core sub‑grid – rows and columns strictly inside the bounding rectangle
core_cell(R, C) :-
    input(R, C, V), V != 0,
    R > Rmin,
    R < Rmax,
    C > Cmin,
    C < Cmax.

% Output: replace non‑zero cells inside the core by the appropriate colour
output(R, C, maxc) :-
    core_cell(R, C),
    input(R, C, V), V != 0,
    corner_maxc.          % use maxc when it appears at all corners

output(R, C, secondc) :-
    core_cell(R, C),
    input(R, C, V), V != 0,
    not corner_maxc.      % otherwise use the second maximal colour

output(R, C, 0) :-
    core_cell(R, C),
    input(R, C, 0).

% Exactly one colour per output cell
1 { output(R, C, Colour) : color(Colour) } 1 :- core_cell(R, C).

#show output/3.
